options: No replacement required Directions (Q16–Q23): Reading Comprehension Financial literacy is the ability to understand and use various financial skills, including budgeting, saving, borrowing, and investing. Although these skills shape almost every important decision a person makes, a surprisingly large portion of the population lacks even a basic grasp of them. As a result, many people drift through life reacting to money problems rather than planning ahead. The costs of financial illiteracy are steep. Individuals who do not understand how interest works often take loans they cannot repay, sinking deeper into debt with every passing month. Without a habit of saving, they remain vulnerable to sudden emergencies such as job loss or illness. Worse, those unfamiliar with basic financial concepts are easy targets for fraudsters offering "guaranteed" returns. The benefits of literacy, by contrast, compound over time. A prudent saver who begins investing early allows compound interest to multiply modest sums into substantial wealth over the decades. Understanding risk helps such a person diversify sensibly, weather downturns, and retire with security rather than anxiety. Much of the problem can be traced to education. Schools rarely teach students how to manage money, leaving young adults to learn painful lessons through trial and error. Advocates therefore argue that personal finance should be a formal part of the curriculum. Fortunately, a growing range of digital tools and budgeting apps now makes it easier than ever to track spending and set goals. Ultimately, building a financially literate society requires collective effort from governments, institutions, and individuals alike. Small, steady steps — recording expenses, comparing interest rates, setting aside a fixed sum each month — can gradually turn anxious spenders into confident, informed decision-makers.
